header.title: Heimskringla 1: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Anonymous
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's urn:menota:anonymous:heimskringla-1:am-35-fol, from the Medieval Nordic Text Archive, Menota (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.4.2: díar (5.22, 6.21), glossed 'priest-chieftains', is a rare word for Odin's twelve temple priests. In Bragi's stanza (7.19-7.26), djúprǫðull ǫðla, rendered 'the deep disc of lands', is a kenning for the land Gefjon ploughed away, and its exact sense is disputed; 'forehead-moons' are the oxen's eyes; víneyjar valrauf, 'the meadow-isle's plunder', is uncertain; hꜹca (7.22) is read as auka, 'increase'. 'Hnir' (4.25, 5.5, 5.7) is read as Hœnir, a letter being lost in the transcription.
notes.9.16: ergi (11.8), rendered 'unmanliness', is a strong term of shame implying sexual passivity in a man; its exact force is disputed. gyðjur (11.9), rendered 'priestesses', can also mean 'goddesses'.
notes.20.14: mara (21.3) is a female night-spirit that rides or tramples sleepers. Finland and the Finns here are the land and people of the Sámi.
notes.13.27: díar (15.4), glossed 'priest-chieftains', is a rare word for Odin's twelve temple priests. Uppsala auðr (15.16), rendered 'the Uppsala estate', is the royal domain attached to Uppsala. 16.21-16.23 play on freyja 'lady' and húsfreyja 'mistress of a household'.
notes.135.31: Bynames: Rettilbeini means 'straight-leg', Ljomi 'gleam'. Verse, in prose order: it is small harm that we, children of old men and old women (common folk), work seiðr, when Rognvald Rettilbeini, Harald's glorious son, works seiðr in Hadeland.
notes.39.17: 'ǫðrum syni sínum' (39.20) is 'his second son', or possibly 'another son of his'. 'Aun's sickness' is death from sheer old age. The last two lines open a stanza by Thjodolf whose subject and verb follow after the unit.
notes.278.17: Gardariki is the Norse name for the lands of the Rus; 'gerzkr' (279.4) means 'from Gardar'. In 279.12-13 the doubt removed is the doubt that the man was a true seer.
notes.285.4: 285.4-5 close a defamatory verse (níð) begun before the unit; 'jǫldu' is 'mare'. The sense of 'úríkr fyrir ríki' ('one powerless in place of / before one mighty') is uncertain.
notes.20.4: 20.4 is the last line of a stanza quoted before the unit, in which the giant-built [hall] of Sokkmimir's [kin] gapes at the prince, Svegdir. 'The Uppsala wealth' is the royal estate attached to Uppsala.
notes.180.10: The sense of 'bragafull' is disputed: 'the toast of the foremost [man]', or 'Bragi's toast'.
notes.180.22: An obscure stanza from the Sigurdardrapa named in the preceding prose. The first half, begun in the previous line ('no man has ash-cup or box'), seems to say that no man need bring cup or box with him to that place, to the offspring of the wealth-wounder; the 'wealth-wounder' is a generous lord, who gives his wealth away, and the passage praises Earl Sigurd's hospitality. 'The gods beguiled Thjazi' is a mythic aside; the word 'fetz' in that line is unclear and is left untranslated. 'The ruler of the sanctuary' is Sigurd as host of the sacrifices. 'vægja kind' (180.26) is obscure: 'kin' is certain, 'of men' is a guess.
notes.361.15: 361.26 carries an editors' note inside the text, 'FJ; BA: Rauð', recording variant forms of the name (Rauði / Rauð); it is not translated.

nodes.text: lie beyond all settlement, there flows
a river through Sweden which is rightly
called Tanais. It was
formerly called Tanakvisl
or Vanakvisl; it comes to
the sea in the Black Sea. At
Vanakvislar it was then called
Vanaland or Vanaheim. That
river divides the thirds of the world. It is called
on the east side Asia, and on the
west side Europe.
II. Of the people of Asia.
East of Tanakvisl, in
Asia, it was called Asaland or
Asaheim. And the chief city which
was in the land they called
Asgard. And in the city was a chieftain
who was called Odin. There
was a great place of sacrifice. It was
the custom there that twelve temple priests were highest;
they were to direct the sacrifices and
judgments between men. These are *díar* [priest-chieftains],
so called, or lords; to them service
and reverence were to be given by all the people.
Odin was a great warrior and very
widely travelled, and won many kingdoms.
many half-years.
III. Chapter. Of Odin's brothers.
Odin had two brothers; one was called
Vé and the other Vili. These brothers of his governed
the realm when he was away. It
happened once, when Odin had gone far
away and had stayed away long, that
the Æsir thought his return home hopeless; then
his brothers began to divide his inheritance. And
his wife Frigg they both took
as theirs. But a little later Odin came
home; he then took back his wife.
Chapter IV. War with the Vanir.
Odin went with an army against
the Vanir, but they met it well and
defended their land, and now one side, now the other had
victory. Each raided the other's land
and did damage. But when it wearied both
sides, they arranged between
themselves a peace meeting and made peace and
exchanged hostages. The Vanir handed over their
most excellent men, Njord the
Wealthy and his son Frey. And
the Æsir in return [gave] the one named Hœnir,
and they declared him very well suited
to be a chieftain. He was a big man
and most handsome. With him the Æsir sent
the one called Mimir, the wisest of men,
and the Vanir gave in return the one who
was cleverest in their company; he was called
Kvasir. And when Hœnir came to Vanaheim
he was at once made a chieftain; Mimir
advised him in everything. But when Hœnir
was present at assemblies or meetings
where Mimir was not near, and there came
some difficult matter before him, then
he always answered the same: 'Let others decide,'
he said. Then the Vanir suspected that the Æsir
must have cheated them in the exchange
of men. Then they seized Mimir and
cut off his head, and sent the head to the Æsir.
Odin took the head and smeared [it] with herbs
so that it could not rot, and
chanted spells over it and gave it such power
that it spoke with him and told him
many hidden things. Njord and
Frey Odin appointed as sacrificial priests, and they were
*díar* [priest-chieftains] among the Æsir. Njord's daughter
was Freyja; she was a sacrificial priestess.
She first taught among
the Æsir *seiðr* [a kind of sorcery], as among the Vanir was
the custom. When Njord was among
the Vanir, he had married a sister
of his own, for that was the law there.
Their children were Frey and Freyja. But
it was forbidden among the Æsir to marry
such close kin.
5. Chapter V. Of Gefjon.
A great mountain range runs from the north-east
to the south-west; it divides Sweden
the Great from other realms. South of
the mountains it is not far to Turkland.
There Odin had great possessions. At that
time the Roman leaders were travelling widely
over the world and subjecting
all peoples to themselves. And many chieftains
fled from that warfare, away from their
lands. And because Odin
had foresight and was skilled in magic,
he knew that his descendants
would in the northern half of the world
settle. Then he set his brothers
Vé and Vili over Asgard,
and he went, and all the *díar* with
him, and a great host of people. He went
first west into Gardariki and
then south into Saxony. He had
many sons. He won realms
far and wide across Saxony, and set there
his sons to guard the land. Then
he went north to the sea, and took
himself a dwelling on an island; the place is now called
Odinsey, on Funen. Then he sent
Gefjon north over the Sound in search
of land. She came to Gylfi, and
he gave her one ploughland. Then
she went to Jotunheim and bore there
four sons to a certain giant. She
turned them into the shape of oxen and yoked them
to the plough and drew the land out into
the sea and west, opposite Odinsey,
and it is called Zealand. There she lived
afterwards. Skjold married her,
the son of Odin. They lived at Lejre.
There a lake or sea is left behind; it is called
Lögrinn. The inlets lie in the lake
just as the headlands in Zealand. So said Bragi
the Old:
Gefjon drew from Gylfi,
glad, the deep disc of lands,
so that from the running draught-beasts
steam rose: Denmark's increase.
The oxen bore, and eight
forehead-moons, where they went
ahead of the meadow-isle's wide
plunder, four heads.
And when Odin learned that good lands
were to be had east with Gylfi, he went
there, and he and Gylfi made a settlement
between them, because Gylfi thought he had no strength
to stand against the Æsir.
Odin and Gylfi contended much with each other in tricks
and illusions, and the Æsir always proved
the stronger. Odin took himself a dwelling by
Lögrinn, at the place now called
Old Sigtuna, and made there a great temple
and sacrifices after the custom of the Æsir. He took possession
there of lands as far as
he called Sigtuna. He gave dwellings
to the temple priests. Njord lived
at Noatun, and Frey at Uppsala,
Heimdall at Himinbjorg,
Thor at Thrudvang, Baldr at
Breidablik. To all of them he gave
good homesteads.
Chapter VI. Of Odin's accomplishments.
When Odin of the Æsir came to the northern lands
He and his temple priests are called song-smiths,
because that art began
with them in the northern lands. Odin
could bring it about that in battle
his enemies became blind or deaf or terror-struck,
and their weapons bit no
more than sticks; but his men went
without mail-coats and were mad as
dogs or wolves, bit into their shields,
were strong as bears or bulls.
They slew people, and
neither fire nor iron had any effect on them.
That is called going berserk.
Chapter VII. Of Odin's skills.
Odin changed shapes; then his body lay
as if asleep or dead, while he was
then a bird or beast, a fish or serpent, and
went in a single instant to far-off
lands on his own errands or other men's.
He could also do this: with words
alone quench fire and calm the sea,
and turn the winds whichever way he
wished. And he had a ship called Skidbladnir,
on which he went over great seas, and
it could be folded up like a cloth.
Odin had with him Mimir's head, and
it told him many tidings from
other worlds; and sometimes he woke
dead men up out of the earth, or sat
beneath hanged men; for this he was called
lord of the dead or lord of the hanged.
He had two ravens which he had
taught to speak; they flew far over
lands and told him many tidings.
From these things he became greatly
learned. All these skills
he taught with runes and songs,
those that are called incantations; for this reason
the Æsir are called smiths of incantations.
Odin knew the art which carries the greatest
power, and practised it himself; it
is called *seiðr* [sorcery]. And by it he could know
the fates of men and things yet to happen; also
bring men death or misfortune
or ill health; also take from men
wit or strength and give [it] to others. But
this sorcery, when it is practised, brings with it
such *ergi* [unmanliness] that it was not thought fit for
men to have dealings with it, and the priestesses were taught
that art. Odin knew of all treasure in the earth,
where it was hidden, and he knew
the songs by which the earth opened up before him,
and the hills and rocks and burial mounds,
and with words alone he bound those
who dwelt within, and went in and took there
whatever he wished. Through these powers
he became very famous. His enemies
feared him, and his friends trusted
in him and believed in his power and
in himself. And he taught most of
his skills to the sacrificial priests; they were
next to him in all lore and
sorcery. Many others, though, learned
much of it, and from there has spread
the sorcery widely, and it has lasted long.
And Odin and those twelve chieftains people worshipped
and called their gods, and believed
be burned, and that there be borne onto the pyre with
them their property. He said this, that
with such wealth should
each man come to Valhalla as
he had on the pyre, and he should
also enjoy what he himself had
Chapter 9. Njord's marriage.
Njord took a wife who
was called Skadi. She would not live with him as his wife,
and afterwards married Odin. They had
many sons. One of them was called Saeming.
About him Eyvind Skaldaspillir composed
many tidings.
X. Odin's death.
Odin died of sickness in Sweden.
And when he was near death,
he had himself marked with a spear-point, and
claimed for himself all men who died by weapons.
He said he would go to Godheim
and welcome his friends there. Now
the Swedes believed that he had come into
the old Asgard and would there
live forever. Then began anew
belief in Odin and vows to him. Often
it seemed to the Swedes that he appeared to them before great
battles took place; to some he then gave
victory, and others he invited to
himself; both lots were thought good.
Odin was burned when dead, and that
burning was made very splendid. It was
their belief that the higher the smoke
rose up into the air, the
more exalted in heaven would be the one whose
burning it was, and the richer,
the more wealth burned with him.
Chapter XI. Of Njord.
Njord of Noatun then became
ruler over the Swedes, and kept
up the sacrifices. The Swedes then called him
their lord. He then received tribute
from them. In his days there was peace,
very good, and plenty of every kind, so great
that the Swedes believed that Njord had power
over the harvest and over men's wealth. In his days
most of the *díar* [priest-chieftains] died, and all were given sacrifice and
burned afterwards. Njord died of sickness;
he too had himself marked for Odin before he died. The Swedes burned him and wept very
much over his grave.
Chapter XII. Frey's death.
Frey then took the kingdom after Njord.
He was called lord over the Swedes and
received tribute from them. He was
well liked and blessed with good harvests, like his father.
Frey raised a great temple at Uppsala
and made his chief seat there; he gave
to it all his dues, lands and
movable wealth. Then the Uppsala estate began,
and it has been kept ever since. In his
days the Peace of Frodi began; then there were
also good harvests in all lands. The Swedes credited
that to Frey; he was the more worshipped
than the other gods, as in his days
the people of the land became richer
than before through the peace and good harvests. Gerd,
Gymir's daughter, was his wife's name. Their son
was called Fjolnir. Frey was called Yngvi
by another name. The name Yngvi was
long afterwards used in his line as
a title of honour, and his kinsmen were afterwards
called Ynglings. Frey fell sick,
and when the sickness gained on him, men sought
a plan, and let few men come to him,
and they built a great mound and
put a door in it and three windows. And when
Frey was dead, they carried him secretly
into the mound, and told the Swedes
that he was alive, and kept him
there three winters; and all the tribute they poured
into the mound: through one window the gold,
and through the second the silver, through the
third copper pennies. Then good harvests
and peace continued.
XIII. Of Freyja and her daughters.
Freyja then kept up
the sacrifices, because she alone survived
then of the gods, and she became
then the most renowned, so that
by her name should be called all
women of rank, just as they are now called
*frúvor* [ladies]. So too each woman is called *freyja* [lady]
over her own property, and she *húsfreyja* [mistress of the house] who
owns a household. Freyja was rather
fickle. Her husband was called Od.
Her daughters were called Hnoss and Gersemi;
they were very beautiful. From
their names the most precious
treasures are so called. When all the Swedes knew
that Frey was dead, and yet there continued
good harvests and peace, they believed that it would
be so as long as Frey was in Sweden,
and they would not burn him, and
called him god of the world, and sacrificed to him most of all
for good harvests and peace for all time after.
Chapter XIV. The death of King Fjolnir.
Fjolnir, son of Yngvi-Frey, then ruled
when Svegdir went from the drinking to
his sleeping-chamber, he looked toward the stone [and saw] that
a dwarf sat under the stone. Svegdir
and his men were very drunk, and they ran
to the stone. The dwarf stood in
gaped at the prince.
Chapter 16. Of Vanlandi.
Vanlandi was the name of Svegdir's son, who
took the kingdom after him and ruled over the Uppsala
wealth. He was a great warrior, and he travelled
back within three winters. But
he did not come in ten winters. Then
Drifa sent for Huld the sorceress, and
sent Visbur, her son and Vanlandi's,
to Sweden. Drifa bargained with
Huld the sorceress that she should
draw Vanlandi by sorcery to Finland,
or else kill him. And
when the sorcery was performed, Vanlandi was
at Uppsala. Then he grew
eager to go to Finland. But
his friends and counsellors forbade him
and said that it must be the sorcery
of the Finns in his eagerness. Then he grew
heavy with sleep, and he lay down to
sleep. But when he had slept only a little,
he cried out and said that a *mara* [night-hag] was trampling
him. His men went to him and wanted to help him.
But when they took hold up at his head,
she trampled his legs so that they nearly
broke. Then they took hold of his feet;
then she pressed down on his head so that there
he died. The Swedes took his body, and he was
burned by a river called Skuta. There
be the death of the best man
in his line, and they went away home.
Then once more *seiðr* [sorcery] was procured and worked,
so that they might be able to kill
their father. Then Huld the seeress told
them that she would work *seiðr* so, and
with this besides, that kin-slayings would always
be in the line of the Ynglings from then on. They
agreed to that. After that they gathered
a force and came upon Visbur by night
Visbur, and ruled the lands. In his days
there came famine and want in Sweden. Then
the Swedes held great sacrifices at Uppsala.
The first autumn they sacrificed oxen,
and the harvests grew no better for that.
the king was no warrior, and he sat
quietly at home on his lands. He was very
rich, and miserly with his wealth. He had
at his court many entertainers of every kind,
harpers, and *gígja*-players [players of a stringed instrument], and fiddlers.
He also had with him sorcerers and all kinds of
folk skilled in witchcraft. Haki and
Hagbard were the names of brothers, and they were very
renowned. They were sea-kings and had a force
Ali's fall King Aun went back to
Uppsala and ruled the kingdom there for another
twenty-five [years]. Then he held a great sacrifice and
sacrificed his second son. Then
Odin told him that he would
live for ever, as long as he gave Odin one of his sons
every tenth year, and this
besides, that he should give a name
to some district in his land after
the number of his sons whom he sacrificed
to Odin. But when he
had sacrificed seven of his sons,
he lived ten winters such that he
could not walk; he was then carried on
a chair. Then he sacrificed his
eighth son, and he lived then another
ten winters and lay then bedridden.
Then he sacrificed
his ninth son, and lived then another ten winters;
then he drank from a horn like an infant.
Then [he] had one son left, and
he wanted then to sacrifice him, and then
he wanted to give Odin Uppsala and the
districts that belong to it, and have it called
the Tenth Land. The Swedes forbade
him that, and then there was no sacrifice. Afterwards
King Aun died, and he is buried in a mound
at Uppsala. Since then it has been called Aun's
sickness if a man dies without ailment of
old age. So says Thjodolf:
Once did,
at Uppsala,
Gunnhild, and said that her father
lived in Halogaland; he
was called Ozur Toti. 'I have been here
for this,' she says, 'to learn magic
from two Finns who are here
the most knowing in the forest. Now they have
gone hunting, and both of them want
to have me, and both are so skilled
that they follow tracks like hounds,
both on thawed ground and on hard snow. And
they go so well on skis that
nothing can escape them, neither men
nor beasts; and whatever they shoot
at, they hit. So they have destroyed
every man who has come here
near, and if they grow angry
the earth turns over before their
eyes. And if any living thing comes
before their eyes, it falls down dead.
Now you must by no
means come in their way, unless I
then try whether we can kill
them. They agreed to this, that she hid
them. She took a linen sack, and
they thought there were ashes in it. She took
some of it in her hand and sprinkled it about the hut,
outside and in. A little later
the Finns come in. They ask what
has come there. She says that nothing
has come. The Finns think that strange,
since they had followed the tracks all [the way]
to the hut, but after that they find
nothing. Then they make themselves a fire and prepare food,
and when they were fed, Gunnhild makes up
her bed. Now it had gone so
for three nights before, that Gunnhild has
slept, but each of them has kept watch
over the other out of jealousy.
Then she said: Come here now,
and lie down on either side of me,
each of you two. They were, at this,
glad, and did so. She held
a hand round the neck of each
of them. They fall asleep at once, but she
wakes them, and soon again they fall asleep,
and so fast that she
can hardly wake them, and again
they fall asleep, and then she can by
no means wake them. And then she sets
them up, and still they sleep.
She then takes two big sealskin bags
and pulls them over their heads and ties
them fast below the arms. Then
she gives a signal to the king's men. They run
forward then and bring weapons against
King Harald also wanted it to be. They were,
father and son, together for long periods. Rognvald
Rettilbeini held Hadeland.
He learned sorcery and became a *seiðmaðr* [practitioner of *seiðr*, sorcery].
King Harald held *seiðr*-men to be evil.
In Hordaland there was a *seiðr*-man who was called
Vitgeir. The king sent him word and bade
him give up *seiðr*. He answers and recites:
That is small harm
that we work *seiðr*,
children of old men
and of old women,
when Rognvald works *seiðr*,
Rettilbeini,
Harald's glorious son,
in Hadeland.
And when King Harald heard this told, then with
his counsel Eirik Bloodaxe went to
the Uplands and came to Hadeland. He burned
his brother Rognvald inside [his house] with eighty
sorcerers, and that deed was much praised.
Gudrod Ljomi was during the winter
with Thjodolf in Hvinir, his foster-father,
Njord's toast and Frey's toast, for good harvest and peace.
Then it was customary for many men to drink
next the *bragafull* [toast of the foremost]. Men drank
also toasts to their kinsmen, those who had been laid
in mounds, and these were called *minni* [memorial toasts].
the offspring, with him to that place,
of the wealth-wounder, to bring;
the gods beguiled Thjazi.
Who would, with the ruler of the sanctuary,
of the kin [of men], contend?
it was also the case that the king sat in the high seat,
his own. And when the first toast
had been poured, Earl Sigurd spoke the words over it and
dedicated it to Odin and drank from the horn
to the king. The king took it and made a cross
sign over it. Then Kar of Gryting said:
Why does the king act so now? Will he
still not sacrifice? Earl Sigurd answers: The king does
as all those do who trust in their might
and main, and dedicate their toast
to Thor. He made the sign of the hammer over it
before he drank. Then all was quiet
through the evening. The next day, when
men went to table, the farmers thronged
the time when he came to the Scillies.
Chapter 31. King Olaf Tryggvason is baptised in the Scillies.
Olaf Tryggvason, when he lay in the Scillies,
heard that there on the island
was a certain seer, who foretold
things not yet come to pass, and many men thought
that it mostly came true. Olaf grew
curious to test the prophecy
of this man. He sent the one of his men
who was handsomest and biggest, and dressed
him as splendidly as could be, and told him to say
that he was the king; for Olaf had
by then become famous for this throughout all
lands, that he was handsomer and nobler
and bigger than all other men. But
since he left Gardariki he had
kept no more of his name, but called
himself Oli and said he was from Gardar. And when
the messenger came to the seer and said he
was the king, he got this answer:
You are not the king, but my advice is that
you be true to your king. He says no more
to this man. The messenger goes back and
tells Olaf. He was all the more eager to meet
this man when he heard such
an answer from him, and now his doubt was removed
that he might not be a seer. Then Olaf went
to meet him and had talk with him, and asked
what the seer would foretell for Olaf
all that could be got away. Then
the Danish king meant to sail that force to
Iceland and avenge the *níð* [defamatory verse] with which all
the Icelanders had defamed him. It
had been made law in Iceland that there should be composed
about the Danish king a *níð* verse
for every nose there was in the land. And
the cause of it was that a ship which Icelandic
men owned was wrecked in Denmark,
and the Danes seized all the goods and called [it]
then people saw, in a mare,
one powerless in place of one mighty.
King Harald told a man skilled in magic to go
in a changed shape to Iceland and find out
what he could tell him. He went
in the shape of a whale. And when he came to the land,
he went west along the north of the land.
He saw that all the mountains and hills
were full of land-spirits, some
big and some small. And when he
came off Vopnafjord, he went
into the fjord and meant to go
ashore. Then down out of
the valley came a great dragon, and with
it came many serpents, toads and lizards,
and they blew venom at him. But he swam
away and west along the land, all the way to
Eyjafjord. He went in along that
fjord. There a bird came against him,
so big that its wings reached
the mountains on both sides, and
a host of other birds, both large
and small. He went away from there
and west around the land, and so south
into Breidafjord, and headed there
into the fjord. There came against him
a great bull, and it waded out into the sea
and began to bellow terribly; a host of
land-spirits followed it. Away

LXVIII. The burning of the sorcerers.
King Olaf then went to Tunsberg
and held an assembly there again, and declared
at the assembly that all those men who
were known and proven to
deal in spells and witchcraft, or were sorcerers,
should all go out of the land
and away. Then the king had a search made
for those men throughout the settlements
that were nearby there, and summoned
them all to him. And when they came
there, there was one man among them who
is named Eyvind Kelda. He was
the grandson of Rognvald Straight-leg, the son
of Harald Fairhair. Eyvind was a sorcerer
and very greatly skilled in magic.
King Olaf had all these men placed
in one hall, and had it well
furnished; he had a feast made for them there
and gave them strong drink. And
when they were drunk, Olaf had fire
set to the hall, and that hall burned
and all the people who were inside it, except that
Eyvind Kelda got out through
the smoke-hole and so away. And when he
prepared for him an Easter feast. He
had nearly three hundred men. That same night
Eyvind Kelda came there to the island. He
had a longship fully manned; they were
all sorcerers and other witchcraft
folk. Eyvind went ashore from the ship, and
his band, and they worked up their sorcery.
Eyvind made for them a concealing
helm and a darkness of fog so great
that the king and his men should not be able
to see them. But when they had come almost
up to the farm at Ogvaldsnes,
then it became bright day. It then turned out very
otherwise than Eyvind had intended. Then
the murk which he had made with
sorcery came over him and his company,
so that they saw no more with their eyes
than with the backs of their heads, and went all round in a ring and
circle. And the king's watchmen saw where
they were going, and did not know what troop that
was. Then it was told to the king. He stood
up, and all his men, and dressed. And when the king
saw where Eyvind and his men were going, he told his
men to arm themselves and go there and find out
what men those were. And when the king's men recognised
Eyvind there, they took him
prisoner, and all of them, and led them
to the king. Then Eyvind told all that had happened
on his journeys. Afterwards the king had them taken,
all of them, and carried out onto a skerry that floods at high tide,
and bound there. Thus Eyvind lost
his life, and all of them. It has since been
called Wizards' Skerry.
Chapter 74. Of the assembly in Trondheim.
King Olaf went with all his force
into Trondheim. And when he came in to
Mære, there had come there all the
chieftains of the Trondheimers who then stood
most against Christianity, and they had
a few men with him, and a few of the farmers.
And when the king came to where the gods
were, Thor sat there, and he was the most
honoured of all the gods, adorned
with gold and silver. King Olaf raised
up a gold-adorned staff which he had
the king threatened him with maiming or death.
Eyvind was not moved by that. Then
the king had a basin brought in, full of
glowing embers, and set on Eyvind's belly.
Soon his belly burst open. Then
Eyvind said: Take the basin off me;
I want to speak some words before
I die. And so it was done. Then
the king asked: Will you now, Eyvind, believe
in Christ? No, he says, I can receive no
baptism. I am a spirit brought to life
in a man's body by the sorcery
of Finns, and my father and mother
had not been able to have a child before. Then
Eyvind died, and he had been the
most skilled in sorcery of men.
